645.title: The Epiphany
645.hook: the magi's gifts: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for death
645.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Epiphany on January 6 or, in the United States and some other countries, on the Sunday between January 2 and 8; some families have their homes blessed and chalk the doorframe that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary, Mother of God, who kept all these words in her heart. Your line was begin with her. Did you stop and ponder before starting something? Day six hundred forty-five.

In early January, above some front doors in Poland, in Germany, in Catholic neighborhoods of the American Midwest, there are letters and numbers chalked on the frame: the year, split in two, with C, M and B in between and little crosses. The letters stand for a Latin blessing, Christ bless this house, and for the three names legend gave the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. The chalk goes up on today's feast. And much of the popular picture of those three men isn't in the Bible.
screen: `CHALK ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `C, M, B.` → `NOT IN THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Matthew calls them magoi, magi, a word Greek writers used for Persian priests and star-watchers. He never says there were three, and he never calls them kings. Later tradition counted three from the three gifts, borrowed crowns from a psalm about kings bringing presents, and gave them names. What Matthew does say: they came from the east, following a star, asking, where is he that is born king of the Jews? They find the child with Mary his mother, they fall down and adore him, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh." Early Christian writers read the gifts as a little creed. Gold, for a king. Frankincense, the incense burned in the temple, for God. Myrrh, a resin used to anoint the dead, for a man who would die. In three boxes, the whole life: royalty, divinity, and a burial. Myrrh comes back at the end of John's gospel, when Nicodemus brings a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, to the tomb. Epiphany comes from the Greek epiphaneia, an appearing or showing. The feast celebrates God made visible, and here made visible to outsiders: foreigners, not of Israel, who read the sky and came a long way. In the Latin West the feast centers on the magi. Eastern churches center the same January feast on the baptism in the Jordan, the great showing. It's traditionally kept on January 6, the twelfth day after Christmas, though in the United States it's moved to the Sunday between January 2 and 8.
screen: `MAGI, NOT KINGS, NOT THREE.` · `THEY FELL DOWN AND ADORED.` · `KING, GOD, AND A BURIAL.` · `EPIPHANY: A SHOWING.` · then, large: `GOLD, FRANKINCENSE, AND MYRRH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a gift for someone unexpected. Not your best friend, not someone who gives to you. Someone outside your usual circle: the person who cleans your office, a neighbor you barely know, a coworker from another floor, a stranger far away. Sit and choose one person. Then choose a gift: something small, a note, a coffee, an hour of help. The magi came from outside; let your gift go outside too. If you pray, you can offer it as they did. If you don't, just plan it. The bell holds the time.
The Epiphany. From the Greek for a showing: the feast of the magi, when Christ is made known to the nations. Today's word.
Your line: gold, frankincense, myrrh. Today, give your unexpected gift, and don't explain it unless they ask. Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: The Baptism of the Lord
646.hook: the Christmas season ends at the Jordan
646.tomorrow: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (18–25 January)
646.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Baptism of the Lord on the Sunday after the Epiphany (or the Monday, when the Epiphany falls on January 7 or 8); it ends the Christmas season, and Ordinary Time begins the next day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Epiphany: magi, not kings, and three gifts that told a whole life. Who got your unexpected gift? Day six hundred forty-six.

In some homes, Christmas ends when the tree goes out to the curb, right after New Year's. In the Church it lasts longer, and it doesn't end with a party. It ends at a river. One week the baby is in the manger with magi kneeling. A few days later, on the calendar, he's a grown man of about thirty, wading into the river in a line of people who've come to confess their sins. The next morning the green vestments come out and Ordinary Time begins. Today is the hinge.
screen: `THE TREE AT THE CURB.` → `FROM MANGER TO RIVER.` → `THE HINGE OF THE SEASON.`

segments.voice: John the Baptist was out by the Jordan, calling people to turn their lives around, and plunging them in the river as a sign. The Greek word baptizō means to dip or immerse. Then Jesus walks up and gets in line. Matthew says John tried to stop him. In the Douay-Rheims: "I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?" It's a real question, and readers still ask it. If Jesus had no sin, why would he go through a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers that it's fitting, to fulfill all justice, and John lets him. Catholic tradition has given several answers to the why. He stood in line with sinners, in solidarity, taking his place among them. He went down into the water not to be made clean but to make the waters holy, so that later baptisms would carry his life. Then the moment itself: he comes up out of the water, the heavens open, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Christian tradition sees all three here: the Son in the river, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice. Notice when the voice comes. Before any miracle, before any sermon, before he's done a single public thing. In Matthew's order, the voice comes first, then the work. For Catholics, that's the shape of every baptism too: the person is claimed and loved before they've accomplished anything. The Christmas season ends here because Christmas was about God showing up; the baptism is where the grown man steps forward.
screen: `BAPTIZŌ: TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `JOHN TRIES TO STOP HIM.` · `NOT TO BE CLEANSED, BUT TO BLESS.` · `THE VOICE BEFORE THE WORK.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your baptism, or think about water. If you're baptized, sit and recall what you know of the day: the church, who held you, your godparents' names. Catholics renew their baptismal promises each Easter, saying no to sin and yes to the faith; if you pray, you can quietly say yes again. If you're not baptized, or would rather not say, simply wash your hands slowly, or touch a little water, and remember the order in the story: the voice before the work. The bell holds the time.
Baptizo, to dip. The Greek root of baptism: Jesus wading into the Jordan with sinners, the feast that closes the Christmas season. Today's word.
Your line: the season ends in water. Today, each time you touch water, at a sink, in the shower, with a glass, remember the river. Day six hundred forty-six.

647.title: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (18–25 January)
647.hook: Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants pray together
647.tomorrow: The Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January)
647.howItsDone: From January 18 to 25 (or around Pentecost in parts of the southern hemisphere), many Catholic parishes join other churches for shared prayer services using materials prepared jointly by the Vatican and the World Council of Churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptizo, a voice from heaven before any work was done. Your line was the season ends in water. Did the sink remind you of the river? Day six hundred forty-seven.

Picture a small town with three churches on the same street: a Catholic parish, a Lutheran church, a Greek Orthodox church with a dome. Most weeks of the year they run their own schedules, ring their own bells, hold their own bake sales. Then, for one week in January, the doors open sideways. The Lutheran pastor reads at the Catholic Vespers. The Catholic choir sings in the Orthodox church. Someone brings coffee for everyone. It's a strange and moving thing to see, and it has a name, and a start date: January 18.
screen: `THREE CHURCHES, ONE STREET.` → `THE DOORS OPEN SIDEWAYS.` → `JANUARY 18.`

segments.voice: On the night before he died, John's gospel says, Jesus prayed for his followers, and for those who would believe through them: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Within a few centuries the followers had split, and split again: East and West in the Middle Ages, then the Reformation in the West. In 1908, an Episcopal priest in New York, Father Paul Wattson, who had founded a community of friars at Graymoor, began an octave of prayer for Christian unity. The next year he and his community were received into the Catholic Church, and popes encouraged the octave. In the 1930s a French priest, Abbé Paul Couturier, widened it: pray for the unity Christ wills, by the means he wills, so Christians of every church could join without first agreeing on the details. Since 1968, Catholics and the World Council of Churches, which includes many Orthodox and Protestant churches, have prepared the prayers together each year, often written by Christians in a different country. The dates were chosen in an older calendar, from a feast of Peter on January 18 to the conversion of Paul on January 25. In the southern hemisphere, many churches keep the week around Pentecost instead. The Second Vatican Council called this kind of shared prayer the soul of the whole effort toward unity. Real differences remain, and the week doesn't pretend otherwise. Each church keeps its own teaching. But for eight days, people who disagree about a great deal stand in the same room and pray the same Our Father.
screen: `THE PRAYER THE NIGHT BEFORE.` · `1908: AN OCTAVE AT GRAYMOOR.` · `UNITY AS CHRIST WILLS.` · `PETER TO PAUL, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with another Christian, or reach across one divide. If you're Christian, think of someone from a different church: a Baptist cousin, an Orthodox coworker, a Catholic neighbor. Plan to pray one Our Father with them this week, or simply to ask how they pray. If you're not Christian, think of one person on the other side of a divide in your own life. Sit and hold them without arguing in your head. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own words, that they may be one. The bell holds the time.
Wattson, the priest. Father Paul Wattson, an Episcopal priest in New York who began an octave of prayer for Christian unity in 1908. Today's word.
Your line: that they may be one. Today, say one kind, true thing about a church that isn't yours. Day six hundred forty-seven.

648.title: The Conversion of Saint Paul (25 January)
648.hook: the unity week ends with the Damascus road
648.howItsDone: Catholics keep January 25 as the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, which also closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, often with an ecumenical Vespers in Rome at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wattson, from Peter's feast to Paul's. Your line was that they may be one. What kind, true thing did you say? Day six hundred forty-eight.

Look at the famous paintings of this scene, Caravaggio's for one, and you'll see a man flat on his back in the dirt, arms thrown up, and a huge horse standing over him. It's the picture that stuck: Paul knocked off his horse. But Acts never mentions a horse. Not once, in any of the three times the story is told. The artists added it. What Acts does give us is stranger than a fall from a saddle, and the unity week ends on it.
screen: `FLAT ON HIS BACK.` → `NO HORSE IN ACTS.` → `STRANGER THAN A FALL.`

segments.voice: Saul of Tarsus was a Pharisee, zealous for his tradition and certain that the followers of Jesus were a danger to it. He had stood by at Stephen's death. Now he gets letters from the high priest to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. On the road, near the city, a light from heaven flashes around him. He falls to the ground and hears a voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Not, why are you persecuting my followers. Me. Saul asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Some readers hear in that single word a seed of what Paul would later write: the Church as the body of Christ, so that what is done to its members is done to him. Saul gets up blind. His companions lead him by the hand into the city, the hunter now helpless, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks. Then the Lord sends a disciple named Ananias, who objects: he has heard how much harm this man has done, and why he has come. He goes anyway, lays hands on him, and calls him brother Saul. Something like scales fall from Saul's eyes, and he is baptized. And one more correction: the conversion doesn't rename him. Acts keeps calling him Saul for several more chapters; only later, on his travels, does it say Saul, who is also called Paul. His conversion has its own feast, and it closes the unity week: the man who set out to break up the community spends the rest of Acts building it.
screen: `LETTERS TO DAMASCUS.` · `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · `BLIND, LED BY THE HAND.` · `ANANIAS SAYS, BROTHER.` · then, large: `I AM JESUS WHOM THOU PERSECUTEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who needs to turn around. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone headed the wrong way: an angry relative, a friend in trouble, a public figure who frightens you. Don't rehearse what they've done. Picture them on a road, and picture a light reaching them. Then think of Ananias, who had to go and call his enemy brother. If you pray, you can pray for that person to turn, and for yourself to be ready when they do. If you don't, simply wish them a road back. The bell holds the time.
Ananias, the disciple. Sent to the blinded Saul in Damascus, frightened but obedient, the one who called him brother and healed his eyes. Today's word.
Your line: the persecutor turned. Today, don't write anyone off. Leave one door open, the way Ananias did. Day six hundred forty-eight.

649.title: Candlemas (2 February)
649.hook: the Presentation: candles blessed for the year, a light to the Gentiles
649.howItsDone: On February 2, the feast of the Presentation of the Lord, Catholic parishes bless candles and may begin Mass with a candlelit procession; some people take blessed candles home for use through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananias: no horse, a light, and a frightened man named Ananias who said brother. Your line was the persecutor turned. Whom did you leave a door open for? Day six hundred forty-nine.

February 2 is Groundhog Day in America: a furry weather forecaster in Pennsylvania, a crowd in the cold, six more weeks of winter or an early spring. The date has an older name. In Europe it was Candlemas, the day people carried candles to church to be blessed, and an old country saying held that a sunny Candlemas meant more winter to come. The usual story is that the groundhog inherited that weather lore. The church kept the candles. Today, forty days after Christmas, a light comes into the temple.
screen: `GROUNDHOG DAY.` → `OLDER WEATHER LORE.` → `FORTY DAYS AFTER CHRISTMAS.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it. Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple in Jerusalem to do what the law of Moses asked: a firstborn son presented to the Lord, and an offering for the mother's purification. They bring a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, which the law allowed for families who couldn't afford a lamb. A poor family, quietly keeping the rules. Then a man named Simeon, who had been told he wouldn't die before seeing the Lord's anointed, takes the child in his arms and blesses God. The Church still sings his words every night at the end of Night Prayer, in Latin called the Nunc dimittis, now dismiss. He says he can go in peace, for his eyes have seen salvation, and he calls the child, in the Douay-Rheims: "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." A light for the nations outside Israel, and glory for Israel itself, both at once. Then he turns to Mary and warns her that a sword will pierce her own soul. And an aged widow named Anna, who never leaves the temple, comes up and speaks of the child to all who are waiting. Tradition ties the day's custom to that line about light. On this day the priest blesses candles, and the people walk into church with them lit, carrying the light the way Simeon carried the child. Some families take blessed candles home to light through the year, during storms, sickness and at the bedside of the dying. Since 1997 it has also been the World Day for Consecrated Life, for nuns, religious brothers and others vowed to God, often seen holding candles today.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, TWO TURTLEDOVES.` · `SIMEON TAKES HIM IN HIS ARMS.` · `A SWORD, AND ANNA.` · `CANDLES CARRIED IN, CARRIED HOME.` · then, large: `A LIGHT TO THE REVELATION OF THE GENTILES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle, blessed if you have one. If there's a candle in your house from church, light it; if not, any candle. Sit with the flame. Think of Simeon, who had waited a long time and then held what he'd been waiting for. What have you been waiting for a long time? Let it be there with the light, without demanding an answer. If you pray, you can pray Simeon's words, now thou dost dismiss thy servant in peace. If you don't, simply let the flame keep you company. The bell holds the time.
Candlemas. The old name for the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, when candles are blessed and carried, forty days after Christmas. Today's word.
Your line: a light to the nations. Today, be some light for someone who isn't in your usual circle. Day six hundred forty-nine.

650.title: Our Lady of Lourdes (11 February)
650.hook: the World Day of the Sick
650.howItsDone: On February 11 Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Lourdes and the World Day of the Sick; many parishes offer the Anointing of the Sick, and pilgrims keep coming to Lourdes itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Candlemas: Simeon, holding a baby, saying he could now go in peace. Your line was a light to the nations. Who got a little of your light? Day six hundred fifty.

At Lourdes, in the south of France, the processions run in an unexpected order. At the very front, not bishops, not dignitaries: people in wheelchairs and on rolling stretchers, pushed by volunteers. Everyone else walks behind them, the healthy following the sick. At Lourdes the order of things is turned around. The ones most places send to the back are put first. And the whole shrine grew from a poor, sick girl gathering firewood.
screen: `WHEELCHAIRS AT THE FRONT.` → `THE ORDER TURNED AROUND.` → `A GIRL GATHERING FIREWOOD.`

segments.voice: Her name was Bernadette Soubirous. She was a teenager, often sick, barely schooled, and her family was so poor they lived in a single room that had once been the town jail. On February 11, 1858, she went with her sister and a friend to gather wood near a grotto by the river, called Massabielle. There, she said, she saw a young lady dressed in white, with a blue sash and a rosary. Through that spring and into July, Bernadette reported the lady coming again and again. The lady asked for prayer and penance for sinners, and for a chapel. Once she told Bernadette to dig in the mud at the back of the grotto; a trickle came up, and it became the spring that still flows there. On March 25, when Bernadette asked her name, the lady answered in the local dialect, in words that are usually given as: I am the Immaculate Conception. Bernadette didn't know what the phrase meant. The parish priest, who had been skeptical, did. Pope Pius IX had defined that teaching only a few years before, in 1854. The bishop approved the apparitions in 1862. Bernadette herself never stayed for the crowds. She became a nun, lived quietly, and died young, still often sick. Pilgrims still come in great numbers. The Church has formally recognized only a small number of healings there as miraculous, after long medical review, and the sick keep coming anyway, to pray, to bathe, to be put first. In 1992 Pope John Paul II made February 11 the World Day of the Sick.

Picture one person who is ill right now: in a hospital, in a care home, at home with something long and tiring. Picture their room. What would it mean to them to hear from you? Decide: a visit, a call, a card, a meal at the door. Pick a time. If you pray, you can ask Our Lady of Lourdes to be with them. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention. The bell holds the time.
Bernadette, the girl. Bernadette Soubirous, the poor, often sick teenager who reported seeing Mary at the grotto of Massabielle in 1858. Today's word.
Your line: the sick come first. Today, make the visit or the call before anything optional on your list. Day six hundred fifty.

651.title: Ash Wednesday (Joel 2:12–18)
651.hook: rend your hearts and not your garments
651.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics receive ashes on the forehead, made from the previous year's blessed palms, and keep a day of fasting and abstinence from meat; it is not a holy day of obligation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette, where the wheelchairs lead the procession. Your line was the sick come first. Did you make the call or the visit? Day six hundred fifty-one.

On one Wednesday every year, people walk around cities with a dark smudge on their foreheads. On the subway, at the office, in the grocery line. Coworkers lean in and say, you've got something on your face. It isn't a holy day of obligation; nobody is required to go. And yet people line up, at lunch hour, before work, after school, to be told in ash that they are dust. Lent starts here.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE SUBWAY.` → `NOT REQUIRED, YET THEY COME.` → `LENT STARTS HERE.`

segments.voice: The first reading is the prophet Joel. A disaster has hit the land, a plague of locusts, and Joel calls the whole people to turn back to God with fasting, weeping and mourning. Then he adds the line that keeps it from becoming theater. In the Douay-Rheims: "And rend your hearts, and not your garments." In the ancient world, tearing your clothes was the public sign of grief. Joel says: tear the inside instead. Then the reason to hope: God is gracious and merciful, patient and rich in mercy. Joel even calls for the newlyweds to leave their wedding chamber; nobody is too busy for this. The gospel that day, from Matthew 6, says almost the same thing: when you give, pray or fast, do it in secret, and wash your face so no one can tell. And then everyone goes up and gets a visible mark on their face. The Church holds that tension on purpose. The ashes are made by burning last year's palms from Palm Sunday. The priest marks a cross and says one of two things: Repent, and believe in the Gospel. Or the older words from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast today, one full meal, and those fourteen and up skip meat. And now this week, looking back: the magi's gold, frankincense and myrrh; the season ending in water; that they may be one; the persecutor turned; a light to the nations; the sick come first. Seven days that walked from Christmas into Lent.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose something to give up, quietly. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing that takes more of you than it should: a habit, a screen, a snack, a tone of voice. Pick it, and decide to let it go for Lent, or even just this week. Then the hard part: tell no one. No posts, no announcements. Let it be between you and God, or between you and yourself. If you pray, you can offer it. Either way, rend your heart a little, not your garments. The bell holds the time.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, when Catholics receive ashes on the forehead and hear: remember that you are dust. Today's word.
Your line: rend your hearts. Today, keep your sacrifice secret, and let it change the inside first. Day six hundred fifty-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ash Wednesday is about the smudge.
what it means: the start of Lent, a call to turn the heart back to God, marked with ash.
what a scholar hears: Joel's call follows a locust plague; garment-tearing was the ancient grief sign, and the day's gospel (Matthew 6) asks for secrecy even as the forehead is marked.
